identity.title: Delayed and diminished carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus)

technique.how: Palpate one carotid artery at a time with the fingertips below the angle of the jaw while auscultating the apex or watching S1; judge whether the pulse rises slowly and peaks late in systole (tardus) and whether its volume is small (parvus). Compare with your expectation for a brisk, sharp upstroke; check both sides sequentially.
technique.prerequisites: Patient supine or semi-recumbent and relaxed; never compress both carotids simultaneously.
technique.contraindications: Known carotid bruit or carotid disease, recent TIA/stroke, or carotid sinus hypersensitivity - palpate gently or omit.

interpretation.positive_finding: A slow-rising, low-volume carotid pulse substantially raises the probability of moderate-or-greater aortic stenosis (pooled LR+ ~9; RCE range 2.8-130).
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal brisk carotid upstroke only modestly lowers the probability (pooled LR- ~0.46, sensitivity ~57%); it does not exclude significant AS, especially in the elderly with stiff arteries.
interpretation.pitfalls: Arterial stiffness in the elderly and hypertension can normalize the upstroke despite severe AS, whereas a low-output state can produce a small pulse without AS; HCM typically gives a brisk, sometimes bisferiens, carotid pulse, which helps separate it from valvular AS.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: request echocardiography and manage as probable significant AS pending results. Negative: does not exclude AS; rely on murmur radiation and A2 to decide on echo.

estimates.target_condition: Aortic stenosis of at least moderate severity
estimates.population: 815 patients in 6 observational studies (mostly murmur/referral populations) examined before echo or left heart catheterization

sources.citation: Bedside Physical Examination for the Diagnosis of Aortic Stenosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. CJC Open. 2024 (PMC10290951).
Etchells E, Bell C, Robb K. Does this patient have an abnormal systolic murmur? JAMA. 1997;277(7):564-571.
Etchells E, Glenns V, Shadowitz S, Bell C, Siu S. A bedside clinical prediction rule for detecting moderate or severe aortic stenosis. J Gen Intern Med. 1998;13(10):699-704.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use to exclude AS in elderly or hypertensive patients with stiff arteries, or to grade severity; do not palpate firmly in patients with carotid bruits or recent cerebrovascular events.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Delayed upstroke with exertional syncope, angina or heart failure suggests severe AS - urgent echocardiography, avoid vasodilators/nitrates and hypovolemia.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Poor reliability: kappa 0.26 for delayed carotid upstroke in the only study reporting it (Etchells 1998, as cited in CJC Open 2024).

extraction_notes: Primary estimate from the 2024 CJC Open meta-analysis (Table 2 seen in PMC full text, 6 studies/815 patients; pooled DOR 13.81 with random effects and possible publication bias from Aronow 1987 and Gamaza-Chulian). RCE 1997 range (2.8-130) added as a second entry with the low end as value and an explicit note - not averaged; RCE full text unavailable so per-study 2x2s not visible. Etchells 1998 (internists, inpatients) reports the upstroke only within a 3-4 finding rule (LR 40, 95% CI 6.6-240), so it is cited but not entered as an estimate for the isolated sign.
verification_notes: [owner fix] removed estimate [1] "Aortic stenosis" - LR+ 2.8 is the low end of the between-study range 2.8-130 in the Etchells 1997 abstract, not a point estimate; the pooled value for this finding is LR+ 9.04
